Maybe The Crooked Man will only appeal to hardcore Hellboy fans who want to see another adaptation of their favorite character, but it is also a very enjoyable riff on folk horror and The Evil Dead with some comic book flourishes.
It respects its source to a high degree – actors are cast (or made up) exactly to resemble Corben’s grotesque faces – and at least manages to evoke proper dread.
Nothing in The Crooked Man compels us to feel invested in this story, which lacks suspense, dramatic momentum and a sense of pacing.
Brian Taylor's Hellboy: The Crooked Man certainly strives to feel different from the previous movies, but comes with the cost of also feeling dry.
Hellboy: The Crooked Man makes a valiant effort to adapt Mike Mignola’s 2008 comic, but ultimately, it falters under the weight of its changes.
Not every superhero adventure has to be a mega-dollar bloat. Here is a B-movie true to the spirit of its source material.
But whereas previous Hellboy movie outings have been colorful, boisterous affairs, Hellboy: The Crooked Man never rises above being a dimly lit, bargain-basement offering.
When committed to the horror component, the film works well enough. Still, the time between “scares,” let alone the minimal amount of action, leaves much to be desired.

While the attempt at building a mysterious and creepy atmosphere around Hellboy is admirable, the execution is lackluster across the board. The editing is clunky, the interactions are awkward, and the pacing is too slow to get any momentum going.
Taylor shoots a couple of excellent moments of body horror too and effectively drives home the mood and atmosphere of a tight, taught, tense tale.
Unfortunately, the finished product is a mess: Poorly paced, confused, boring, and just so ugly.
If you're expecting the kinetic stylings of a Marvel or a DC offering – or even del Toro's 2004 film – you might get a little frustrated. But I think The Crooked Man will find its own fans – in time.

It’s not horrible because it’s offensively incompetent, but rather because it had an intriguing concept, a good source and a solid cast, and it used it all to develop a tedious, at times incoherent and disappointing experience. Full review in Spanish.

It’s immediately evident what a decidedly low-budget affair this entry is, and despite its relative faithfulness to the Mignola’s comic, it never really transcends its obvious direct-to-streaming pedigree.
Hellboy: The Crooked Man’s accuracy is a double-edged sword.
It’s all too much. The horrors are piled on in such quantities that any possibility of being scared or even slightly repulsed soon evaporates.

Hellboy: The Crooked Man misses its mark and its periodic successes aren’t enough to justify this disappointing experience. Seasoned Hellboy fans will feel robbed of a substantial story and curious genre fans will be left wondering what they just watched.
Taylor envisions a Hellboy where the horror matters more than the humor or poetry or romance or even the good vibes, and he’s made a film that proves his take is valid.
